lead: Both readings speak of belonging. Paul tells the Corinthians that their bodies belong to the Lord, bought at a price and made a temple of the Holy Spirit, and will be raised by God’s power. In John, Jesus promises that whoever the Father gives him he will never drive away, and that he will raise them up on the last day. The body that receives Christ is not a thing we may use as we like; it is held in the hands of the One who will raise it.

set: Corinth was a busy port city, known in the ancient world for loose living. Some Christians there seem to have taken Paul’s teaching on freedom from the Law and turned it into a slogan, “All things are lawful for me.” They may also have thought that what the body does does not touch the soul. Paul answers with the faith of the Church: the body belongs to the Lord, it will rise, and the Spirit dwells in it.
str: vv. 12–14: two Corinthian slogans answered: not all things are beneficial; the body is for the Lord, and God will raise it.
vv. 15–17: your bodies are members of Christ; union with a prostitute contradicts union with the Lord.
v. 18: shun fornication, a sin against one’s own body.
vv. 19–20: the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit; you were bought with a price; glorify God in your body.
¶ The NRSV prints the Corinthian slogans in quotation marks. Greek manuscripts have no quotation marks, but most scholars agree that Paul is quoting his readers here.
kw: For Paul the body is not a shell for the soul; it is the whole person in his visible, bodily life. That is why he can say that the body is “for the Lord” and will be raised.
The inner shrine where God dwells, not the whole temple area. Paul used the word for the whole community (3:16); here he uses it for each Christian’s body.
A word of the market place, used of buying a slave. Christians were bought at the price of Christ’s blood (1 Peter 1:18–19), and now belong to a new and loving Master.
vv: “All things are lawful for me,” but not all things are beneficial.
Paul does not deny Christian freedom. He asks what it is for. A freedom that makes us slaves of our appetites has destroyed itself.
And God raised the Lord and will also raise us by his power.
The resurrection of the body is the reason for Christian moral life. What God will raise must not be treated as worthless.
Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, which you have from God, and that you are not your own?
The Spirit is not a guest in the soul only. He dwells in the whole person, body included.
For you were bought with a price; therefore glorify God in your body.
Chastity, care for health, modesty and work are all ways to glorify God in the body.
ch: The Catechism quotes this passage when it teaches the resurrection of the body: the body is meant for the Lord, and the Lord for the body; your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit; you are not your own; so glorify God in your body (CCC 1004). It also teaches that the human body shares in the dignity of the image of God and is intended to become, in the Body of Christ, a temple of the Spirit (CCC 364). On this ground the Church teaches chastity for every state of life, married and unmarried, as the integration of sexuality within the person (CCC 2337, 2348).

set: Jesus is speaking at Capernaum, the day after the feeding of the five thousand. The crowd has asked for a sign like the manna, and he has answered, “I am the bread of life” (6:35). Now he speaks of the Father’s will: that none whom the Father gives him should be lost. When some of the crowd grumble, he tells them that coming to him is itself the Father’s gift.
str: vv. 37–40: the Father’s will: all he gives will come; none will be lost; all who believe will be raised on the last day.
vv. 41–42: the crowd complains: is not this the son of Joseph?
vv. 43–44: no one can come unless drawn by the Father; and I will raise that person up.
kw: A strong double negative in Greek: I will surely not throw out. Whoever comes to Christ, however poor or sinful, is not turned away.
Words of the same root are used in the Greek Old Testament for Israel grumbling against Moses in the wilderness over food (Exodus 16:2, 7). The scene of the manna is being lived again.
A strong word, used for drawing a net full of fish (21:6, 11). The Father draws people to the Son, and the Son will draw all people to himself when he is lifted up (12:32).
vv: Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and anyone who comes to me I will never drive away
Two truths stand side by side: God’s gift and our coming. Grace does not cancel our freedom; it makes our coming possible.
And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day.
Four times in this chapter Jesus promises to raise up on the last day (6:39, 40, 44, 54). Eternal life begins now in faith and reaches its fullness in the resurrection of the body.
No one can come to me unless drawn by the Father who sent me
The first step toward Christ is never only our own. Every desire for God is already God at work in us.
ch: St Augustine, commenting on verse 44, asks how anyone can be drawn if he comes of his own will, and answers that we are drawn not by force but by delight and love, as a sheep is drawn by a green branch held out to it (in substance, Tractates on John 26). The Catechism teaches that the preparation of man for grace is already a work of grace, and that God’s initiative calls for man’s response in freedom (CCC 2001–2002). John’s “the Jews” in verse 41 means here the Galilean crowd that questions Jesus, not the Jewish people as a whole; Jesus and his disciples were themselves Jews, and the Church warns against reading such words as blame on the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).

qa: If no one can come unless the Father draws him, are some people not drawn at all?

The Church teaches that God “desires everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4), and that Christ died for all without exception (CCC 605). The Father draws all; but his drawing is not force, and a person can resist it. Jesus’ words warn the grumblers not to trust in their own judgment, “whose father and mother we know”, but to let God teach them.
study: Paul says, “you are not your own.” How does this truth change the way I treat my body and the bodies of others?
Jesus says he will never drive away anyone who comes to him. Who in my family or parish needs to hear this today?
